2. Short back ground facts, relevant for the disposal of the Rule, are that one Rezaul Karim Khan, Assistant Sub-Inspector of Police of Shahbagh Police Station, Dhaka, as informant, lodged an FIR on 21-8-2007 under Rules 3(4) and 6(2) of the Emergency Powers Rules, 2007 ("EPR 2007") against the convict-petitioners along with 15 (fifteen) others alleging, inter-alia, that on 21-8-2007, in the morning, while he was on patrol duty along with other police personnel in Dhaka University area, some four to five thousands violent students assembled in front of the Arts Building and Modhur Canteen of the Dhaka University and held processions and demonstrations against the Emergency proclaimed by the then government; that as the informant and other police personnel tried to resist them, they started pelting bricks and went berserk with lathi etc.; that some teachers of the Dhaka University joined the said processions as well and they created obstructions against police in performing their official duties, damaged several vehicles and created a reign of terror in the Dhaka University area. Upon above FIR, Shahabagh Police Station Case No. 53 dated 21-8-2007 was registered, and police commenced investigation and submitted charge-sheet, being Charge-Sheet No. 298 dated 8-9-2007, under Rules 3(4) and 6(2) of EPR-2007 against the petitioners along with 15(fifteen) other accused. The case was then transferred to the Court of Druto Bichar Adalat No.4, Dhaka, presided over by a Metropolitan Magistrate, for trial, and the trial court, on 12-12-2007, framed charge against the petitioners and others under Rules 3(4) and 6(2) of EPR-2007, in absence of the petitioners. During trial, the prosecution examined sixteen witnesses, and the trial Court, by judgment and order dated 21-1-2008, acquitted all the accused except the petitioners, who were convicted in absentia and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of taka 1000, in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one month more. However, the sentences against the petitioners having been remitted/pardoned by the Hon'ble President of Bangladesh on the very day of judgment in exercise of his power under Article 49 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, the petitioners preferred Appeal, being Criminal Appeal No. 155 of 2008, under Rule 11 of the EPR 2007 before the Court of Metropolitan Sessions Judge, Dhaka only against the impugned order of conviction, whereupon the learned Metropolitan Sessions Judge, Dhaka (the Appellate Court) dismissed the said appeal summarily by the impugned judgment and order dated 18-3-2008. The petitioners then moved this Court and obtained the aforesaid Rule through application under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 4. Mr Asaduzzaman, learned advocate appearing for the convict-petitioners, at the very outset, submits that the very basis of the impugned judgment and order of the Appellate Court below is misconceived inasmuch as that after the remission of the sentences against the petitioners by the Hon'ble President, they were no more fugitive on the day the appeal was presented and, as such, the Appellate Court below committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice in dismissing the said appeal summarily mainly on the ground that the petitioners were fugitive from law during trial and as such, they were not entitled to any relief. Referring to the relevant orders passed by the Trial Court, in particular the orders dated 21-1-2008 and 22-1-2008, Mr Asad points out that since all the processes as issued by the Trial Court were recalled on 22-1-2008, the very next day the judgment of conviction and sentences was pronounced, the presence of the petitioners before the Court or any authority physically were not required anymore thereafter, and, as such„ the Appellate Court committed illegality in terming them fugitive from law. Mr Asad further submits that when the petitioners, upon obtaining certified copies, preferred appeal before the Appellate Court below in compliance with the relevant provisions of the EPR 2007 and Code of Criminal Procedure, the Appellate Court ought not to have rejected the said appeal summarily. Further, referring to various parts of the judgment as passed by the trial Court convicting the petitioners as well as the depositions of the witnesses, in particular the deposition PW 7, Mr Asad submits that the judgment of conviction as passed by the Trial Court cannot even sustain in the eye of law in-as-much-as that the conviction was solely based on the deposition one witness, namely PW-7, who was a chance witness and whose whereabouts were not known to the Trial Court or not even dis-closed to the Court though he was a highly interested witness. 

 5. Mr KM Zahid Sarwar, learned DAG representing the State, on the other hand, submits that although the Hon'ble President remit-ted the sentences of the petitioners, they were still required to surrender before Court below, and by not doing so, they became fugitive in the eye of law and, as such, do not deserve any order in their favour from this Court of law in view of the long established principle of law as settled by this Court in various cases including Chand Shah vs Crown 8 DLR (PC) 24, Anti-Corruption Commission vs Mahmud Hossain; 61 DLR (AD) 72, Anti-Corruption Commission vs ATM Nazimullah Chowdhury, 62 DLR (AD) 225, Anti-Corruption Commission vs Dr HBM lqbal Alamgir 15 BLC (AD) 45. Relying on a recently decided case of this Court in Sarwar Kamal vs State; 64 DLR 329 ("Sarwar Kamal's case"), Mr Sarwar submits that in a similar situation in that case the High Court Division refused any relief to the petitioner under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure on the ground that he was a fugitive from law as he did not surrender before the Trial Court even though his sentence was remitted by the Hon'ble President. Further, drawing our attention to the deposition of PW7 and the depositions of other witnesses, Mr Sarwar submits that though only one witness, namely PW 7, mentioned the names of the petitioners implicating them in the offences, the Courts below committed no illegality in relying on the said sole witness as it is lawful to convict on the basis of the deposition of one witness only, if found trustworthy. Therefore, he submits, this Court should not interfere into the impugned judgment of conviction. 

 6. Considered the submissions of the learned advocates, perused the application as well as the materials on record, including the lower court records which are available before us. Let us first address whether the petitioners were fugitive from law and were entitled to relief from the Appellate Court below on the day when they preferred Criminal Appeal No. 155 of 2008. It is the admitted position that the trial of the case was held in absence of the petitioners. It is also on record that on the day the trial Court delivered the judgment, i.e., on 21-1-2008, the Gazette reemitting the entire sentences and penalties of the petitioners by the Hon'ble President was published. It further appears from the record of the trial Court that the fact of such remission of sentences and penalties was somehow communicated to the learned Judge of the Trial Court, who, accordingly, took note of the same in the order sheet on 22-1-2008 in the following terms:— 

 7. Since a similar issue was dealt with by this Court very recently in Sarwar Kamal's case as cited by the learned Deputy Attorney General, we have examined the said decision. In Sarwar Kamal's case, the convict Sarwar Kamal preferred appeal before the High Court Division against his conviction and sentence and he was on bail. After hearing, the High Court Division dismissed his appeal and accordingly directed him to surrender before the trial Court. Thereafter, as the Hon'ble President remitted his sentence on an application already filed by his wife, he refrained from surrendering as per the direction of the High Court Division. His learned Advocate rather drew the trial Court's attention to the fact of pardon by the President and prayed for recall of Warrant of Conviction and Arrest. However, the trail court rejected the said prayer holding that since Mr Sarwar Kamal did not surrender pursuant to the direction of the High Court Division after dismissal of his appeal, he became fugitive from law, and without such surrender, he was not entitled to get any relief from the Court. Being aggrieved, Mr Sarwar Kamal then filed an application before the High Court Division under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure seeking a direction on the trial Court to implement the order of pardon/remission granted by the Hon'ble President. The High Court Division, rejecting the said application, upheld the position taken by the trial court. Although in Sarwar Kamal's case the Rule was under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the concerned Bench of this Court questioned the very propriety of pardon or remission itself as granted by the Hon'ble President and finally declared the same to be unlawful. 

 8. Since the facts of the case before us and the Sarwar Kamal's case are different, we are refraining from discussing that case in detail as that would be mere academic. What is relevant is that in Sarwar Kamal's case, the High Court Division specifically directed MrSarwar Kamal to surrender before the trial Court, which he did not comply, and on that ground the trial Court as well as the High Court Division termed him fugitive from law. However, in the case before us, there was no such direction from any Court of law except the processes issued by the trial Court itself, namely the process issued during trail and the Warrants of Conviction and Arrest issued on the very day when it pronounced the judgment of conviction and sentence. But on the following day, i.e. on 22-1-2008, all such processes were recalled. Therefore, we do not find any defiance of law or direction of the Court in this case on the part of the petitioners at list when the appeal preferred by them was presented before the Appellate Court. Since the trial court below recalled the Warrant of Arrest and Conviction on 22-1-2008 pursuant to the pardon/remission granted by the Hon'ble President on the previous day under any stretch of imagination, the petitioners cannot be termed or called as 'fugitive from law at list from 22-1-2008 on wards. However, it appears from impugned order of the appellate Court below that the appeal was summarily rejected mainly on the ground that the petitioners were fugitive from law during trial. Whatever may be their status during the trial, they were at least not fugitive from law on 22-1-2008 on wards as their entire sentences were remitted by the Hon'ble President in the meantime and the processes issued by the trial Court requiring the presence of their bodies were recalled by the trial Court itself. Therefore, physically they were not required to remain present or surrender before any Court of law and, as such, they cannot be termed fugitive and denied relief on the day their appeal was presented before the learned Sessions Judge for admission. 

 9. It further appears that the Appellate Court cited another reason for not entertaining the appeal, namely that the certified copies of the depositions of prosecution witnesses were not submitted by the petitioners along with the Petition of Appeal. We do not find any reason as to why such position was taken by the learned Sessions Judge in particular when section 419 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which was made applicable by the "EPR 2007", requires only copy of judgment to be accompanied with the Petition of Appeal. Section 419 further provides that even the requirement of such submission of the copy of the judgment appealed against may be exempted, by the Appellate Court. In any case, the learned Sessions Judge was supposed to send for the records of the case upon admission of appeal in view of the provisions under section 423 of the Code. Absurd as it is, the learned Sessions Judge even found fault in the petitioners as they had failed to submit the certified copies of the return of process issued by the trial court under sections 87 and 88 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, when those could have been made available upon admission of the appeal and calling for the records of the trial court. 

 11. We have also considered the depositions of the witnesses as recorded by the trial Court below, in particular the deposition of PW 7, Md Ahsanullah, as well as relevant depositions of the prosecution witnesses. The deposition of PW 7 reveals that he was in fact a chance witness. He admitted that he had finished his study in Dhaka University in 2003, left the residential hall in 2006 and started residing at another address. He does not mention any reason as to why and how he was present at the place of occurrence on the very day of 28th August, 2007 and subsequently. He even does not explain as to how he knew the petitioners and how he collected their names as he was no more a student of Dhaka University at the relevant time and left the residential hall one year back. It was the onus of the prosecution as well as this witness to justify his presence at the place of occurrence at the relevant time and as to how he knew the identities of the petitioners, which they failed to discharge miserably. When he claimed to be present tt it the campus of Dhaka University on the 28 August, 2007, he failed to disclose anything as to how he remained present as such when the entire campus was burning due to the agitation of the students of the Dhaka University compelling the then government to clamp curfew. Therefore, we are of the considered view that any conviction solely relying on the disclosure of names by a chance witness like PW 7 will be highly unsafe and against the very tenor of rule of evidence making it not sustainable in law. 

 12. Though the appellate Court below questioned the absence of the petitioners during the entire trial, it has to be borne in mind that the trial was being conducted at a time when the country was under emergency. This Court can take those facts into consideration that no reasonable man would present himself happily before any Court or members of law enforcing agencies during that time fearing undue exercise of power. Therefore, even if they were absent during the entire trial, they ought not to have been convicted merely on the basis of such abscondance. 

 Since we are of the view that it was very much unsafe on the part of the trial Court to convict the petitioners solely on the basis of the deposition of a chance witness like PW 7 and that the petitioners were not fugitive from law at list on 22-1-2008 and thereafter, we do not find any legal reason to allow this conviction to sustain. Accordingly, this Rule, issued under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, should succeed. 

 Send down the lower Court records at once.
